title: Tone and the author's attitude
blurb: Separate a word's dictionary meaning from the feeling it carries, and use word choice to name an author's tone precisely.
question: Two reviewers describe the same nurse. One calls her “assertive”; the other calls her “aggressive.” The words share a dictionary meaning, so why do the reviews feel so different, and what tone does each reviewer take?

teach.body: Every word has a denotation, its literal dictionary meaning, and a connotation, the emotional or cultural association it carries: positive, negative or neutral. “Thrifty,” “frugal” and “cheap” all denote spending little money. But thrifty sounds wise, frugal sounds neutral, and cheap sounds mean. Plain English: denotation is what a word says; connotation is how it makes you feel about what it says.

teach.caption: All three describe someone who spends little. The connotation decides whether the writer approves.

head: Positive
Neutral
Negative
teach.caption: On the HESI A2, a trap option often has the right denotation and the wrong connotation.

teach.body: Tone is the author's attitude toward the subject. Authors rarely announce it; they reveal it through the connotations of their word choices. A writer who calls a policy “bold” and “overdue” is approving; one who calls it “reckless” and “rushed” is critical. To name the tone, collect the charged words, decide whether they lean positive or negative, and then choose the most precise tone word that fits all of them.

teach.caption: Humorous, ironic and urgent can attach to any attitude: decide from the passage.
“What is the author's tone?” never has a topic for its answer, and “frightening” describes a mood, not an attitude.

teach.body: Andre, a nursing applicant, reads this editorial: “The hospital board says its new wait-time dashboard will ‘transform the patient experience.’ Perhaps. The screen does show average waits, updated hourly. But the board made similar promises about a triage desk in 2019 and a text-alert system in 2021, and waits grew longer after both. Patients may want to see results before they celebrate.”

items: Collect the charged words: “Perhaps.” (a one-word doubt), “similar promises,” “waits grew longer,” “before they celebrate.”
Sort them: all lean toward doubt, none toward anger or praise.
Reject “objective”: the dates and facts are there, but the word choice clearly takes a side.
Reject “indignant”: nothing is angry or outraged.
Choose the precise word: the author doubts the claim until proof arrives. The tone is skeptical.

teach.text: Four tone traps: an option with the right denotation but the wrong connotation (“stubborn” for an admiring description of “determined”); calling a passage “objective” because it contains dates or statistics when its word choice is slanted; a tone matched to the topic (a passage about a serious illness is not “pessimistic” unless the author expects bad outcomes); and picking a mood, a topic or a purpose (“to inform”) when the question asks for the author's attitude.

items: Denotation: the literal dictionary meaning. Connotation: the positive, negative or neutral feeling attached.
Know the families: thrifty/frugal/cheap, assertive/aggressive, childlike/childish, curious/nosy.
Tone is the author's attitude, revealed by the connotations of word choices.
Tone is not mood (the reader's feeling) and not topic (the subject).
Pick the most precise tone word that fits every charged word in the passage.

summary: You can now separate a word's denotation from its connotation and rank word families from positive to negative. You can also name an author's tone precisely from word choice, without confusing tone with mood or topic.

A.q: Which word has the most negative connotation?
A.why: All four words denote spending little, but “stingy” suggests a mean unwillingness to share, a clearly negative connotation.

whyNot.0: “Thrifty” suggests wise, careful spending: a positive connotation.
whyNot.1: “Economical” suggests efficiency and is neutral to positive.
whyNot.3: “Frugal” is largely neutral: it describes spending little without judging it.

A.q: A care-home report describes a resident as “stubborn” about walking to meals instead of “determined.” Both words mean unwilling to give up. What does the word change alter?
options: The denotation, from positive to negative
The connotation, from positive to negative
The topic, from walking to stubbornness
The purpose, from informing to persuading
A.why: The two words share a denotation (unwilling to give up). Swapping “determined” for “stubborn” changes only the connotation, from admiring to disapproving.

whyNot.0: Denotation is the shared dictionary meaning, which stays the same; the feeling is what changes.
whyNot.2: The report is still about the resident walking to meals; one word does not change the subject.
whyNot.3: The report still exists to inform; one word choice signals the writer's attitude, not a new purpose.

A.q: “At last, after eleven years of bake sales, raffles and car washes, the Eastside neighborhood has its own health center. Neighbors packed the ribbon-cutting, and the applause lasted nearly a full minute.” Which word best describes the author's tone?
A.why: “At last,” a packed ribbon-cutting and a minute of applause all carry positive, triumphant connotations. The tone is celebratory.

whyNot.0: The eleven years are mentioned, but the author celebrates the present achievement rather than longing for the past.
whyNot.1: Nothing in the passage doubts the center or its value.
whyNot.2: A matter-of-fact tone is plain and unemotional; “At last” and the vivid applause show the author's pleasure.

B.q: “The new intern is a know-it-all in staff meetings.” Which revision gives the sentence a positive connotation without changing its basic meaning?
options: The new intern is a show-off in staff meetings.
The new intern is a smart aleck in staff meetings.
The new intern is uninformed in staff meetings.
The new intern is well-informed in staff meetings.
B.why: “Well-informed” keeps the denotation (knows a great deal) but carries a positive connotation instead of the negative “know-it-all.”

whyNot.0: “Show-off” is still negative; it suggests bragging for attention.
whyNot.1: “Smart aleck” is still negative; it suggests rude cleverness.
whyNot.2: “Uninformed” changes the denotation: it means not knowing, the opposite idea.

B.q: “The city's new parking app is truly a marvel: it takes just nine taps, two password resets and a call to customer service to pay for a fifteen-minute spot.” Which word best describes the author's tone?
B.why: The author calls the app “a marvel” while listing frustrating steps. Saying the opposite of what is meant to mock something is sarcasm.

whyNot.0: The praise is not sincere: the details show the app is a hassle.
whyNot.1: “Truly a marvel” is a judgment, and the details are chosen to ridicule.
whyNot.3: Pessimism expects a bad future; this mocks a present problem.

B.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes tone from mood?
options: Tone is the author's attitude; mood is the reader's feeling
Tone is the reader's feeling; mood is the author's attitude
Tone is the passage's subject; mood is the author's purpose
Tone is a word's literal meaning; mood is its connotation
B.why: Tone belongs to the author (an attitude toward the subject); mood is the feeling the text creates in the reader.

whyNot.2: The subject is the topic, and purpose is why the author writes; neither is tone or mood.
whyNot.3: Literal meaning is denotation; tone and mood are not word-level meanings.

C.q: “For three winters, a crew of tireless volunteers has kept the warming shelter on Fifth Street open every night, cooking hot meals and folding donated blankets.” What does the word “tireless” suggest about the author's view of the volunteers?
options: Negative; the author thinks they overwork
Neutral; the author is reporting their hours
Positive; the author admires their effort
Negative; the author pities their exhaustion
C.why: “Tireless” has a positive connotation of energetic dedication. Combined with the details of nightly meals and blankets, it shows admiration.

whyNot.0: Nothing in the sentence criticizes the volunteers' workload; the details are praiseworthy.
whyNot.1: No hours are given, and “tireless” is a judgment, not a measurement.
whyNot.3: “Tireless” means NOT tired, so it cannot suggest exhaustion.

C.q: “A supplement company says its new sleep gummy ‘works for everyone.’ Maybe so. The label does list melatonin and chamomile, and the company cites a study of 30 adults. But that study lasted one week, and the company paid for it. Shoppers may want stronger evidence before they buy.” Which word best describes the author's tone?
C.why: “Maybe so” and the pointed details about the short, company-funded study express doubt about the claim. Doubting a claim until it is proven is a skeptical tone.

whyNot.0: Indignant means angry at an injustice; the author questions the claim but does not rage.
whyNot.2: The author advises waiting for stronger evidence, the opposite of celebrating the product.
whyNot.3: The ingredients and study size are factual, but “Maybe so” and the chosen weaknesses show a clear attitude.

C.q: A nurse is writing a discharge note about an 84-year-old patient who insists on dressing and bathing herself. Which word conveys this trait with a positive connotation?
C.why: “Independent” conveys a preference for doing things oneself with a positive, respectful connotation.

whyNot.1: “Headstrong” suggests reckless willfulness, a negative connotation.
whyNot.2: “Obstinate” means unreasonably refusing to change, a negative connotation.
whyNot.3: “Uncooperative” frames her as a problem for staff, a negative connotation.

reteach.title: The same photo, three captions
reteach.question: Picture one photo of a crowd outside City Hall. Three newspapers caption it differently. The photo is the denotation; the captions add the connotation.

blocks.body: Caption 1: “Residents gather outside City Hall.” Caption 2: “Concerned residents rally for their neighborhood.” Caption 3: “An angry mob swarms City Hall.” Every caption describes the same people standing in the same place. What changes is the feeling each word choice attaches: neutral, positive, negative. Readers sense each newspaper's tone (its attitude) from those choices, just as you will on the HESI A2.

blocks.h: Three captions on the connotation scale

blocks.text: The feeling a caption gives YOU (alarm, pride) is mood. The newspaper's attitude toward the crowd is tone. A tone question asks about the writer, not you.

explain.body: Denotation is the literal dictionary meaning. Connotation is the positive, negative or neutral association. Two words can share a denotation and differ only in connotation: confident and arrogant both describe strong self-belief.

test.q: Which pair of words has nearly the same denotation but opposite connotations?
test.why: Both describe strong belief in oneself; confident is positive and arrogant is negative.

whyNot.0: These have opposite denotations: showing care for others versus failing to.
whyNot.2: These share a denotation AND a positive connotation.
whyNot.3: These are close in meaning and both neutral, so the connotations are not opposite.

explain.body: Word families can be ranked from positive through neutral to negative. Place the neutral word in the middle, then ask which remaining word a writer would use to praise and which to criticize.

test.q: All three words name a smell. Which list orders them from most positive to most negative connotation?
test.why: “Fragrance” suggests a pleasant smell (positive), “odor” is neutral, and “stench” suggests a foul smell (negative).

whyNot.0: This reverses the order, running from negative to positive.
whyNot.1: The neutral word “odor” is placed first, ahead of the positive “fragrance.”
whyNot.2: The negative “stench” is placed in the middle, ahead of the neutral “odor.”

explain.body: Collect the charged words, decide which way they lean, then choose the most precise tone word: objective, critical, skeptical, sarcastic, nostalgic, optimistic, sympathetic, indignant, reverent, and so on.

test.q: “Every Sunday of my childhood, my grandmother's kitchen smelled of cinnamon and coffee. I sat on the tall stool by the window while she hummed old songs. The house was sold years ago, but I still catch that scent in bakeries and stop, just for a moment.” Which word best describes the tone?
test.why: The author fondly recalls a lost past (“years ago,” “I still catch that scent... and stop”). Wistful longing for the past is a nostalgic tone.

whyNot.0: Reverent means deeply respectful or worshipful; the passage is fond and wistful rather than solemn.
whyNot.1: Nothing is being celebrated now; the house is gone and the author is looking back.
whyNot.3: Sensory memories and personal feeling make the passage subjective, not objective.

explain.h: Tone is not mood or topic
explain.body: Tone is the author's attitude. Mood is the feeling the text creates in the reader. Topic is what the passage is about. A tone answer is an attitude word, never a subject.

test.q: A passage describes how a river town rebuilt after a flood, praising neighbors who shared tools and opened their homes. Which choice describes the author's tone rather than the topic or mood?
test.why: “Admiring” is an attitude word that matches the author's praise for the neighbors.

whyNot.1: Flood recovery is the topic of the passage, not an attitude.
whyNot.2: “Frightening” describes a feeling the reader might have (mood), and it does not match the praise.
whyNot.3: Rebuilding is part of the subject matter, not the author's attitude.
